name: Forms
summary: How every form control is labelled, described, marked as required and validated, and how a form reports its errors, on every platform.
description: A form is a set of controls people fill in and submit: text fields, number fields, text areas, selects, checkboxes, radio groups. Each control is specified on its own page; this foundation holds what they share, so that a field behaves the same way next to its neighbours and on every platform: its anatomy (label, description, message), how a required field is marked, which validation statuses exist and how they render, when a value is checked, how errors are announced and summarised, and how fields are spaced. Draft: the rules below describe what the controls do today and what every trusted source agrees on; each open point is decided one step at a time with the team.

rules.name: Anatomy of a field
rules.text: A field stacks a visible label, the control, an optional description (format, example, constraint) and, when validation fails, a message saying what is wrong and how to fix it. A group of checkboxes or radios takes the same parts around its options, with a legend as its label. Today the message is shown under the description; whether it replaces it is not decided yet.

rules.name: Label
rules.text: Every control has a visible label that stays visible while people type, associated with the control so assistive technology announces it as the control's name. A placeholder is never the label.

rules.name: Required fields
rules.text: A required field is exposed as required to assistive technology and marked visibly before people submit, never by color alone. Today the words are left to the author (in the label or the description) and no mark is drawn; the mark itself is not decided yet.

rules.name: Validation statuses
rules.text: Today one status exists, invalid: the control takes the error color and the error message is shown. Whether warning and success statuses exist, and how each renders, is not decided yet.

rules.name: Errors are said in text
rules.text: An error is identified in text next to the control it concerns, associated with that control, and never shown by color alone. The text says what is wrong and, when a fix is known, how to fix it.

rules.name: When a value is checked
rules.text: Not decided yet: on submit, when people leave the field, or as they type. A control is never marked invalid before validation ran.

rules.name: How errors are announced
rules.text: Not decided yet, for each platform: where focus goes after a failed submit, and how an error that appears without a submit reaches assistive technology.

rules.name: Error summary
rules.text: Not decided yet: whether a form lists its errors above the fields, with a link to each field.

rules.name: Spacing
rules.text: Not decided yet: the space between fields, between groups of fields and before the form's actions. Today a field spaces its own parts by its container gap, and a group by its row gap.

rules.name: Web rendering
rules.text: A label element pointing at the control's id; the description and the message referenced by aria-describedby; the required attribute on a required control; aria-invalid on a control that failed validation; a fieldset and its legend around a group of checkboxes or radios.

guidelines.text: Every control has a visible label or instructions, associated with it programmatically.
Related controls are grouped, and the group has a name: a set of radios always, a set of checkboxes or related fields when it helps.
A required field is indicated visibly, not only programmatically and never by color alone; a symbol used to mark it is explained before its first use.
When an input error is detected, the field in error is identified and the error is described in text; color or an icon may add to the text, never replace it.
When a correction is known, the error message suggests it, unless that would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
A control is marked invalid only after its value was validated, not before people used it.
A message that reports errors or a result without moving focus, such as the number of errors in a form, is exposed as a status message so assistive technology announces it.
Validate fields when it makes sense: an email address when people move to another field, a user name or password before they leave it; show errors right next to the field.
Make sure people understand that they must provide the required data before they can continue, for example by enabling the Next or Continue button only once the required fields are filled in.
Expose an error with the error semantics of the field, so the screen reader reads the error with it; announce content that changes without focus with a polite live region.
Error identification, labels or instructions and error suggestion apply to non-web software as they do to web content.

decisions.text: Material's component guidelines (m3.material.io/components/) and Microsoft's Windows app controls guidance and WinUI automation reference are trusted sources, so the form rules for Android and Windows cite those platforms' own guidance.
decisions.rationale: They hold the only Android and Windows guidance on forms (required marking, error text replacing the supporting text, spacing, announcing changes); without them, the foundation could only say these platforms are silent.

changelog.note: Material's component guidelines and Microsoft's Windows app controls guidance become trusted sources for the form rules on Android and Windows (forms-platform-sources).

First draft of the page, to show how the foundation will be represented: rules describing what the form controls do today and what every trusted source agrees on, the open points named as not decided, the status colors measured on every surface level without a minimum while the statuses are decided.
